title: 2 Kings 17:19–23
context: The explanation widens to Judah, which also followed Israel’s ways, and then returns to Israel’s root sin: the division of the kingdom and Jeroboam’s calf worship, which Israel never abandoned. Israel’s removal fulfills what the prophets had said. The words to this day show the narrator writing well after the event.

verses.text: Also Judah didn’t keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah also did not keep the commandments but followed Israel’s ways. Arminian readers note that Judah had the warning of Israel’s fate and still drifted, which makes its responsibility greater.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this verse anticipating Judah’s own exile (2 Kings 25). The narrator writes for a Judean audience who needed to learn from Israel’s fall.

verses.text: The LORD rejected all the offspring of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hands of raiders, until he had cast them out of his sight.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD rejected Israel’s offspring, afflicted them, and gave them to raiders. Arminian readers see judgment unfolding in stages, each one an opportunity to return before the final removal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working through foreign raiders as instruments of judgment. The Judges 9:23 box already discusses how the traditions relate God’s purposes to the actions of such agents.

verses.text: For he tore Israel from David’s house; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king; and Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD, and made them sin a great sin.
verses.arminianNotes: God tore Israel from David’s house, and Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD. Arminian readers note that Jeroboam’s choices had consequences for an entire nation over two centuries.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the division itself came from God (1 Kings 11:31), yet Jeroboam bears responsibility for the idolatry that followed. Divine purpose and human sin both stand in the account.

verses.text: The children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he did; they didn’t depart from them
verses.arminianNotes: Israel walked in Jeroboam’s sins and never departed from them. Arminian readers stress that repentance was always possible but never chosen at the national level.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the persistence of Jeroboam’s pattern as evidence of how deeply sin had rooted itself in the nation’s life. Even Jehu, who destroyed Baal worship, left the calves at Bethel and Dan in place (10:29).

verses.text: until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he said by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was carried away out of their own land to Assyria to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD removed Israel as he had said through the prophets. Arminian readers see the prophetic warnings vindicated, and they note the Deuteronomy 31:21 box on God’s foreknowledge of Israel’s apostasy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled exactly. The phrase to this day reflects the narrator’s perspective long after the exile, when its lessons still applied.
